An analysis1 of the outcome of treatment of 83 915 children found that the risk of hospitalisation for gastrointestinal bleeding, renal failure, or anaphylaxis was no greater in children given ibuprofen than in those given paracetamol. 1. Lesko SM, Mitchell AA. An assessment of the safety of pediatric ibuprofen. JAMA 1995; 273: 929–33. Effects on the blood. Blood disorders including agranulocy- tosis, aplastic anaemia,1 pure white-cell aplasia,2 and thrombocytopenia3 have been reported in patients taking ibupro- fen. Fatal haemolytic anaemia occurred in a man taking ibupro- fen and oxazepam.4 1. Gryfe CI, Rubenzahl S. Agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia possibly due to ibuprofen. Br J Clin Pract 1994; 48: 51. 4. Guidry JB, et al. Fatal autoimmune hemolytic anemia associated with ibuprofen. JAMA 1979; 242: 68–9. Effects on the cardiovascular system. For a discussion of the cardiovascular effects of NSAIDs, including ibuprofen, see p.96. Effects on the CNS. Aseptic meningitis has occurred in pa- tients taking NSAIDs. A review1 of NSAID-related CNS ad- verse effects summarised 23 literature reports of NSAID-associ- ated aseptic meningitis; 17 reports involved ibuprofen, 4 sulindac, 1 naproxen, and 1 tolmetin. Of the 23 reports, 11 were in patients with a diagnosis of SLE. Typically the reaction is seen in patients who have just restarted NSAID therapy after a gap in their treatment.
